text:
I took the dataset from my other page, and worked on it to bring it up to third normal form here.
For this process, I created empty tables for the necessary sorting, and gave them columns with the appropriate data types for what they will hold. 
Then, I inserted unique combinations of the appropriate columns, and connected them together with IDs.



Database Table Configuration


This makes the database much more efficient and standardized for storage and retrieval of data. It also makes it less convenient for my use, of extracting it for analysis. But this is more impressive.

title: analysis
text:
Importing data

data <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT `chicago_2019_2022`.`id`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`crash_date`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`crash_time`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`town`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`crash_severity`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`days_snow`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`temp`,
    `chicago_2019_2022`.`snow`
FROM `new_schema`.`chicago_2019_2022`;
")


grouped <- data %>%
  group_by(temp = round(`temp`)) %>%
    count(temp = round(`temp`), name = "counted")

Car crashes are best avoided, so its worth studying under what conditions they happen. I have a dataset from the city of chicago of crashes occurring from 2019-2022, and associated weather data. I will analyze this, and see if I can conclude certain temperatures are more dangerous than others.

ggplot(data = grouped, aes(x = temp, y = counted)) +
  # Adding transparency (alpha) and color makes overlapping points easier to see
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "dodgerblue4", size = 2) +
  
  # Professional theme to remove unnecessary background clutter
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  
  # Title and descriptive labels
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Distribution in Chicago",
    subtitle = "Frequency of recorded temperatures, 2019–2022",
    x = "Temperature (°F)",
    y = "Frequency (Count)",
    caption = "Data: Chicago Weather Records"
  ) +
  
  # Customizing text styles
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 20)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )








Heres the graph of counts, and there are clear peaks at just below 40 and 80 degrees. More car crashes occur at these temperatures, but is it significantly more likely?

poly_model <- lm(counted ~ poly(temp, 4), data = grouped)
summary(poly_model)


Call:
lm(formula = counted ~ poly(temp, 4), data = grouped)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2685.11  -545.13   -44.65   443.30  3104.88 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)      2947.09      99.37  29.658   <2e-16 ***
poly(temp, 4)1  14471.99    1110.99  13.026   <2e-16 ***
poly(temp, 4)2 -16843.85    1110.99 -15.161   <2e-16 ***
poly(temp, 4)3 -12149.74    1110.99 -10.936   <2e-16 ***
poly(temp, 4)4    171.98    1110.99   0.155    0.877    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1111 on 120 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8123,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.806 
F-statistic: 129.8 on 4 and 120 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


This is a model constructed on the data. with an extremely low p value, it seems there is enough evidence to conclude a relation to the number of crashes occuring while the city is at certain tempreratures.

ggplot(data = grouped, aes(x = temp, y = counted)) +
  # Adding transparency (alpha) and color makes overlapping points easier to see
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "dodgerblue4", size = 2) +
  
  # Professional theme to remove unnecessary background clutter
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  
  # Title and descriptive labels
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Distribution in Chicago",
    subtitle = "Frequency of recorded temperatures, 2019–2022",
    x = "Temperature (°F)",
    y = "Frequency (Count)",
    caption = "Data: Chicago Weather Records"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), 
    color = "firebrick", 
    linewidth = 1.2,
    se = TRUE  # This adds the shaded confidence interval
  ) +
  
  # Customizing text styles
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 20)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    
  )








Well, this is just pointing out the more common temperatures. To really catch it, we need a higher order polynomial line.

ggplot(data = grouped, aes(x = temp, y = counted)) +
  # Adding transparency (alpha) and color makes overlapping points easier to see
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "dodgerblue4", size = 2) +
  
  # Professional theme to remove unnecessary background clutter
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  
  # Title and descriptive labels
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Distribution in Chicago",
    subtitle = "Frequency of recorded temperatures, 2019–2022",
    x = "Temperature (°F)",
    y = "Frequency (Count)",
    caption = "Data: Chicago Weather Records"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 8), 
    color = "firebrick", 
    linewidth = 1.2,
    se = TRUE  # This adds the shaded confidence interval
  ) +
  
  # Customizing text styles
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 20)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    
  )








This fits the data nicely but theres still a problem. Its the more common temperatures are going to be over represented in this method. to solve this, we need to try to put this against how often temperatures occur.

t_high <- function(m) {
  omega <- 2 * pi / 365
  55.75 - 15.54 * sin(omega * m) - 18.38 * cos(omega * m)
}

t_low <- function(m) {
  omega <- 2 * pi / 365
  45.42 - 15.54 * sin(omega * m) - 17.30 * cos(omega * m)
}
m <- 1:365

highs <- round(sapply(m, t_high), 1)
lows  <- round(sapply(m, t_low), 1)

# 1. Input your Chicago graph values
chicago_norms <- data.frame(
  month = 1:365,
  highs = round(sapply(m, t_high), 1),
  lows  = round(sapply(m, t_low), 1)
)



# 2. Estimate hourly distribution for every day of the year
estimated_frequency <- chicago_norms %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  do(data.frame(
    temp = round(seq(.$low, .$high, length.out = 24)) # Simple linear hourly estimate
  )) %>%
  count(temp, name = "estimated_occurrence")
   

normalized_data <- grouped %>%
  left_join(estimated_frequency, by = "temp") %>%
  replace_na(list(estimated_occurrence = 100))

normalized_data$estimated_occurrence = normalized_data$estimated_occurrence+ 100
plot(normalized_data$temp, normalized_data$estimated_occurrence)








Based off of data of the average temperature in chicago from the historical weather almanac, I construct a graph of average minimum and maximum temps, and sample it hourly for every day of the year.

normalized_data$norm = normalized_data$counted /normalized_data$estimated_occurrence
ggplot(data=normalized_data, aes(x = temp,y = norm))+
         geom_point()








By dividing the first graph by the second, we get a rough estimate of the comparative rates of accidents by temperature. As the weights were fairly arbitrary, I have to leave it at that. But this graph supports the idea that car crashes are more common at around 40 and 80 degrees. So be cautious when driving then.
